title: About & references
text:
About this draft
This v0.1 methodological discussion draft presents a causal-assumption framework linking a directed acyclic graph (DAG), an assumption register, and a Summary of Evidence table (SET). The templates, terminology, and reporting examples are proposals for review, not validated guidance or adopted standards. The Briefing sets out the four feedback questions.

title: About & references
text:
Methodological context
Turner RM, Spiegelhalter DJ, Smith GCS, Thompson SG. Bias modelling in evidence synthesis. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series A. 2009;172(1):21–47. Read the paper.
The proposed framework is a qualitative counterpart to quantitative bias modelling: it makes causal structure, stream-specific contributions, connecting assumptions, and possible shared biases explicit. It does not estimate bias parameters or replace quantitative adjustment.

Estimand layer
The estimand specification and alignment guidance draws on:

ICH E9(R1). Addendum on Estimands and Sensitivity Analysis in Clinical Trials. 2019. Guideline.
Kahan BC, Hindley J, Edwards M, Cro S, Morris TP. The estimands framework: a primer on the ICH E9(R1) addendum. BMJ. 2024;384:e076316. Read the paper.
Kahan BC, Devane D. Estimands: what they are and why we should use them. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology. 2026;189:112054. Read the paper.
Keene ON, Lynggaard H, Englert S, Lanius V, Wright D. Why estimands are needed to define treatment effects in clinical trials. BMC Medicine. 2023;21:117. Read the paper.
Kahan BC, Morris TP, White IR, Carpenter J, Cro S. Estimands in published protocols of randomised trials: urgent improvement needed. Trials. 2021;22:202. Read the paper.

The specification and alignment components are new methodological proposals developed alongside this framework; the full drafts are available as downloads and their development is recorded in the project’s background documents.

title: About & references

Applications and evidence

TAAR1: retrospective illustration
The TAAR1 example reconstructs how the framework could have supported a completed review. Its diagram, assumption IDs, and statuses are illustrative retrospective judgements, not records of the original panel using these tools.
The worked SET reports estimates and 95% confidence intervals from the published triangulation and the living systematic review. It is not a current evidence update or an independent audit of those publications.


LSR8: ongoing application
For Heat & Mental Health, the framework is being introduced after protocol completion, while the living systematic reviews are underway. Proposed assumptions and priority adjudications remain open for review; they are not completed meeting conclusions.

Contribution

title: TAAR1 · Retrospective application
text:
Target specification
The register above records assumptions; the target itself also needs stating. The retrospective materials do not contain a fully specified target, so the following is an illustrative completed statement, for calibration only — bracketed content is a placeholder to be confirmed against the actual protocol and trials, not a claim about them:

In [adults with schizophrenia spectrum disorders], what is the [mean difference] in [PANSS total score] at [4–6 weeks] under [add-on TAAR1 agonism at the doses used in the included trials, continued as assigned] compared with [placebo add-on], treating [treatment discontinuation and switching] using a [treatment-policy strategy]?

Even this statement leaves open whether the review’s interest is the assignment effect (as stated), a hypothetical fully-adherent effect, or a mechanistic pathway. The specification worksheet forces that decision into the open; the full guidance is available as a download.

title: Proposal 2 · Triangulation meeting worksheet
text:
Purpose
The worksheet gives the panel a common record of how evidence changes its interpretation of the DAG and its assumptions. The Summary of Evidence table (SET) summarises the evidence; the assumption register records the conditions attached to the interpretation.
See the TAAR1 DAG and register for the worked illustration. The worksheet below turns that reasoning into prompts a meeting can use.

title: Proposal 2 · Triangulation meeting worksheet
text:
Four steps







Step
What the team records




1. Map
The relationship or query each stream informs, the estimate or finding, and the assumptions needed to connect it to the target question.


2. Compare
Whether each stream addresses the target causal question, a related question, or a different link (causal alignment assessment); which integration level that supports — A common effect, B related but non-identical, C different links; where findings agree, diverge, or complement.


3. Examine bias
Shared and differing bias mechanisms, their expected directions, magnitudes, and uncertainty, and the implications for interpretation.


4. Revise and record
The conclusion and its conditions; edge statuses for revised relationships (supported / unsupported / uncertain / not adequately investigated); changes to assumptions or the diagram; unresolved questions and actions.

title: Proposal 2 · Triangulation meeting worksheet
text:
Proposed worksheet fields







Before the discussion
After the discussion




Target question and target specification version; date and participants; diagram, register, and SET versions; evidence already known when the framework was adopted.
Conclusion and conditions; integration level chosen and its rationale; edge statuses for revised relationships; revised versions; actions, owners, and review dates.

title: Proposal 2 · Triangulation meeting worksheet
section: Causal alignment assessment within the four steps
text:
Causal alignment assessment within the four steps
Companion guidance (Component B) supplies the questions and records within each step — no new procedure is needed. Each evidence stream gets a stream-level estimand (the quantity it can estimate in its own terms) prepared before the meeting, so Step 2 compares specified quantities rather than a study with an underspecified ambition.








Step
Component B support
Artefact produced




Preparation
Retrieve the versioned target specification; draft stream-level estimands.
Draft stream-level estimands in the meeting pack


1. Map
Place each contribution on the edge, node, proxy connection or assumption it informs — not automatically a single arrow; classify contribution type.
Contribution map with register IDs


2. Compare
Alignment discussion: did streams estimate the same quantity? Resolve the integration level (A common effect / B related but non-identical / C different links). Distinct from the SET’s indirectness column (applicability).
Below-SET narrative record per stream (draft)


3. Examine bias
Identification, indirectness, transportability; then the orthogonality check — shared vs differing bias mechanisms relative to each stream’s own estimand.
Orthogonality judgement; bias notes keyed to register IDs


4. Revise and record
Conditional interpretation; route each change as alignment re-interpretation, DAG/register update, or formal target amendment.
Final narrative records; versioned updates



Steps 1 and 2 iterate rather than sequence strictly: alignment assessment comes before or alongside mapping, never after cross-stream agreement is declared.


Alignment questions, descriptors, narrative record, and orthogonality check


Opening alignment questions (B1a)

What exactly was the review target, and which version of that specification is being used?
What did the included studies aim to estimate, and can that be inferred confidently from the reports?
What does the synthesis summarise: a common effect, a distribution of study effects, an association, a qualitative pattern, or several distinct results?
What quantity did this stream target in its own terms (the stream-level estimand)? Alignment is judged between two specified quantities, not between a study and an underspecified ambition.
Does the evidence provide an estimate of the target or a contribution that must be interpreted through another assumption or causal pathway?
Could an apparent agreement or discrepancy arise because different quantities were estimated rather than because studies yielded conflicting evidence?

When the review has no numerical target estimand (hypothesis-generating mode): the alignment question shifts from does this quantity match the target quantity? to does this evidence inform the proposed relationship, its measurement, or the assumptions connecting its components? The SEM’s rows are assessed against pathway components rather than a pooled effect.


Dimension-specific signalling questions (B1b)







Dimension
Signalling questions (examples)




Population / setting
Who is represented by the study and synthesis? Who is in the target? Are age, diagnosis, species, severity, context or effect modifiers different?


Intervention / exposure / comparator
Are dose, timing, treatment versions, assignment versus receipt and comparison conditions the same? Is a hypothetical intervention well-defined?


Outcome / construct / measurement
Is the outcome the target construct, a different manifestation or a proxy? Could changes in measurement alter direction or meaning?


Timing
Do exposure period, outcome follow-up, mediator order and treatment duration match?


Quantity / causal effect definition
Is the target descriptive, associative or causal? Total effect, assignment effect, hypothetical adherence effect, direct or mediated effect?


Synthesis target / summary measure
What does the pooled estimate or SWiM summary target? Are measures transformable? Does pooling over studies yield the target-population quantity?


Intercurrent events (where relevant)
How were discontinuation, switching, rescue treatment or competing events handled? Is this compatible with the target?





Descriptive labels (B1c) — provisional language only

Closely aligned: the stream addresses a compatible target quantity, notwithstanding methodological validity and applicability questions.
Partly aligned: substantial correspondence, but a consequential difference or qualification remains.
Different but relevant: the stream addresses a distinct quantity, yet can inform the target through a specified mechanism, proxy, context or assumption.
Connection unclear: reporting or conceptual uncertainty prevents a defensible judgement.
No established link to this target: currently no justified inferential connection; this does not mean the evidence has no other scientific value.

These are descriptors, not categories with validated thresholds, and should not be forced into a global rating.


From alignment judgements to the integration level
The alignment judgements resolve into the integration level for each pair or set of streams, which determines how they may be brought together:

A — Sufficiently common causal effect: streams estimate effects defensibly related to one target estimand → quantitative integration may be possible (transformations, transportability assumptions, bias adjustment).
B — Related but non-identical effects or constructs: streams address closely related questions but cannot defensibly be represented as observations of one target effect → retain within-stream quantitative synthesis; compare across streams without pooling.
C — Different links in a broader causal explanation: streams inform different edges or propositions in the causal model → complementary, pathway-/question-level triangulation; “agreement” is not the operative concept.

The level is a recorded judgement with its rationale, not a score; borderline or mixed cases (for example, closely aligned on intervention, different on outcome) should be described per dimension as above.


Blank narrative record (below the SET table, one per stream row)

SET row and target reference: [review, outcome, target version, synthesis version].
Stream-level estimand: [what this stream targeted in its own terms].
What is being summarised? [one to three sentences on study-level variation and the synthesis target].
Main points of alignment or difference: [key population, contrast, outcome, time and effect-definition considerations].
Why this evidence contributes: [direct/related/mechanistic/contextual/assumption-relevant contribution].
What must be assumed to connect it to the target? [DAG/register references].
Unresolved questions for triangulation: [reporting gaps, validity, transportability, bias and possible challenges].



Orthogonality check (Step 3 support)

List the key bias mechanisms for each stream (selection, measurement, reporting, confounding, analysis) relative to each stream’s own estimand.
Identify mechanisms that could operate in both streams — shared publication practices, shared measurement instruments, shared populations, or animal-to-human assumptions that transmit bias in the same direction.
Ask: if the shared mechanism operated, would it produce the observed pattern of agreement or disagreement?
Record whether the differing-bias premise of the triangulation is justified for this pair of streams, or merely asserted by design labels.

Agreement between streams with plausibly shared bias should be reported as conditional in the same way as agreement resting on a contested proxy assumption.

Download the full estimand alignment guidance (.md)
The Word worksheet provides blank tables and response spaces for these fields and the four steps. It can be completed before and during a meeting, then kept with the review records.


Detailed questions for follow-up


Which fields are essential for the panel, and which can be prepared or maintained elsewhere?
Is the preparation and recording burden justified, and who owns the record between updates?


The four questions on the Briefing page guide the meeting discussion.

title: Concepts: the terms needed for this proposal
text:
The argument
The proposed unit of reasoning is target relationship → stream-specific contribution → connecting assumptions. A cross-stream judgement needs to specify what each stream informs and the conditions under which its findings bear on the target question. Shared bias remains a possible explanation for apparent agreement.
The framework extends familiar within-study DAG reasoning to this between-stream setting. The DAG shows the proposed causal structure; the register records the connecting assumptions; the Summary of Evidence table (SET) links the findings to them. Its role as a qualitative counterpart to quantitative bias modelling is explained in the Briefing.

title: Concepts: the terms needed for this proposal

A worked illustration
The TAAR1 example shows the DAG and its assumption register together. Selected labels identify the proxy connection and the proposed mechanism. The worked evidence summary shows how the register links enter the SET.

title: Concepts: the terms needed for this proposal
text:
Ten terms for this discussion







Term
Working definition




Causal DAG — directed acyclic graph
A diagram of hypothesised direct causal influences, with no directed cycles. Both arrows and omitted arrows encode assumptions.


Assumption register
A versioned record of assumptions with IDs, statements, affected relationships/streams, judgements, rationale, and what could challenge them.


Proxy
A measured variable used to stand in for another construct. Its relevance needs justification; the animal behavioural outcome and human symptom outcome remain distinct.


Estimand
The precisely specified quantity a question seeks: a descriptive quantity, an association parameter (marginal or adjusted), a causal contrast, or — for hypothesis-generating questions — a candidate relationship that may have no single numerical estimand. An estimand can be specified even when the available data cannot identify it.


Causal alignment assessment
A structured judgement of whether the quantity a stream estimates, or the contribution it makes, addresses the review’s target causal question, a related question, or a different link in the causal pathway — and what assumptions are needed to connect it to the target. Distinct from indirectness (applicability of a quantity) and from risk of bias (validity of a quantity for its own estimand). Assessed narratively at the evidence-summary stage; not scored.


Integration level
The level at which evidence streams can legitimately be integrated, determined by the causal alignment assessment: A — sufficiently common causal effect (quantitative integration may be possible); B — related but non-identical effects or constructs (retain within-stream synthesis; compare across streams without pooling); C — different links in a broader causal explanation (complementary, pathway-/question-level triangulation).


Stream-level estimand
The quantity an evidence stream can estimate in its own terms: population, intervention/exposure, comparator, outcome, timing, summary quantity and effect type. Specified before alignment is judged, so that alignment relates two specified quantities — for example, an animal behavioural contrast and a human clinical contrast — rather than a study and an underspecified ambition.


Indirectness / applicability
A difference between the evidence and the target population, exposure/intervention, outcome, timing, or setting that affects its relevance.


SET — Summary of Evidence table
A concise account of findings, bias, applicability, and the assumptions relevant to triangulation.


Bias type — offset versus scaling
Offset (additive / shift) bias adds a distortion and can move a true null. Scaling (proportional / stretch) bias multiplies an effect on the stated scale; a true zero remains zero on that scale.



Alignment is not indirectness. Indirectness asks whether a stream’s estimate applies to the review’s target population, exposure, outcome or setting — a question of applicability of a quantity. Alignment asks whether the stream estimated the review’s target quantity at all — a question of what was estimated, connected to the target only through stated assumptions. A stream can be low in indirectness for its own estimand yet misaligned with the review target (the TAAR1 animal behavioural outcome), or closely aligned in quantity yet indirect for the target population (a trial restricted to adults under 65). The Summary of Evidence table keeps the two judgements in their separate places: indirectness in its existing column, alignment in the narrative below the table.

title: Concepts: the terms needed for this proposal
text:
Reference appendix


Additional methodological terms

These definitions retain the rest of the source glossary for reference.







Term
Working definition




Node
A variable in the diagram, such as exposure, a mediator, or an outcome.


Edge / arrow
An assumed direct causal influence between two nodes. A target question can concern several paths rather than one arrow.


Direct versus total effect
A direct effect excludes pathways through specified mediators; a total effect includes pathways through them. A trial’s total-effect estimate should not automatically be attached to a direct arrow.


Confounder
A variable that causally influences both exposure and outcome, creating a non-causal route between them.


Effect modifier
A characteristic across whose values an effect differs on a specified scale. It is not necessarily a confounder.


Mediator
A variable on a causal pathway, such as exposure → mediator → outcome. Adjusting for it can change the quantity being estimated.


Collider
A variable caused by two other variables. Conditioning on it can open a non-causal path.


Scoping mode versus hypothesis mode
Scoping mode uses the diagram to clarify the question and evidence contributions. Hypothesis mode makes proposed pathways explicit for examination. Record the diagram’s purpose and when it was introduced.


SMD — standardised mean difference
An effect expressed in standard-deviation units. Similar units do not make different outcomes or target quantities equivalent.


Bias direction — towards or away from the null
How a bias is expected to move an estimate relative to the true value, for a specified contrast and scale. Direction may be uncertain or involve crossing the null.


Triangulation
Drawing an interpretation across evidence contributions while examining their different and shared key sources of bias and assumptions.


Orthogonality / differing bias structures
The extent to which key bias mechanisms differ across streams. Independence needs justification; different design labels alone do not establish it.


Causal-assumption framework (“scaffolding”)
The proposed structure connecting the DAG, explicit assumptions, evidence summaries, meeting deliberation, and reporting.


Assumption types
Four proposed categories: structural, identifying, proxy, and indirectness/applicability, defined below.


Structural assumption
A claim about a causal relationship or its absence, such as the proposed dopamine pathway in TAAR1 (A3).


Identifying assumption
A condition needed for a study’s estimate to identify the stated causal quantity, such as sufficient confounding control for an observational contrast.


Proxy assumption
A claim that a measured proxy is informative about the target construct, such as the contested TAAR1 animal-to-human connection (A1).


Indirectness assumption
A claim about the extent to which findings transfer to the target population, intervention/exposure, outcome, or setting.


Target relationship / causal query
The question the review seeks to answer. It may concern an association, a total effect, a direct effect, or a mediated pathway.


Evidence stream
Evidence grouped by a relevant design or inferential approach; distinct identifying assumptions can require separate streams.


Evidence contribution map
A table showing what each stream can inform and which assumptions connect it to the target question.


Decision log
A dated record of changes, reasons, and ownership, linking successive diagram and register versions.


Edge status
The post-synthesis status of a relationship in the causal graph: supported, unsupported, uncertain, or not adequately investigated. Recorded in the decision log when the diagram is revised, paralleling the status judgements in the assumption register.


Evidential contribution type
The role a stream plays relative to the target: direct target contribution, related effect, mechanistic, contextual, or assumption-testing. Classified separately from alignment and risk of bias; a stream may hold several roles, and roles are not tied to particular study designs.


Target version
A dated, versioned statement of the review’s target quantity or question. Amended only when the question is intentionally redefined, with justification and a record of the evidence known at the time. An evidential challenge to a mechanism does not by itself change the target.


SEM — Summary of Evidence on Mediators
The synthesis output of the hypothesis-generating route: a structured summary of evidence on candidate mediator relationships, from which a consensus meeting selects the mediators carried forward. A table, not a diagram — and not a structural equation model.


Causal graph
Umbrella term for DAGs, causal DAGs, path diagrams and related visualisations of assumed relationships between variables. An arrow is a causal claim only when it is given a causal interpretation; a diagram drawn to display associations or statistical model structure functions as a causal graph only under that reading.

title: Making causal assumptions explicit in triangulation
text:
The problem
Cross-stream agreement in triangulation is currently interpreted without making explicit the causal structure, proxy validity, and applicability assumptions that connect each stream to the target question — and shared biases can manufacture apparent agreement.

title: Making causal assumptions explicit in triangulation
text:
The conceptual claim to stress-test

Target relationship → Stream-specific contribution → Connecting assumptions

This is the unit of reasoning I want the team to stress-test: whether it captures what warrants a cross-stream judgement, including when shared bias could explain agreement. The methodological aim is to make that reasoning explicit and reviewable; the templates are its practical application.

title: Making causal assumptions explicit in triangulation
text:
Where this sits methodologically
Directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) are familiar tools for making the assumptions behind confounding control within a study explicit. This proposal extends that logic to the between-stream setting: which target relationship each stream informs, and which identifying, proxy, and applicability assumptions connect its contribution to that target. An estimand layer underpins this: each question and each evidence stream gets a specified target quantity at protocol stage (Component A), and each stream’s quantity is checked for causal alignment with the review target at evidence-summary stage (Component B).

title: Making causal assumptions explicit in triangulation
section: What I mean by the framework
text:
What I mean by the framework
The working notes call this “scaffolding”: a linked set of visual and written tools that helps a team make its assumptions explicit and carry its reasoning between stages of a review.
The DAG visualises the hypothesised causal structure. An assumption register records the assumptions, their rationale, and what could challenge them. The Summary of Evidence table (SET) connects the findings to those assumptions. The three templates guide how the team prepares, discusses, and reports this information.
See the worked TAAR1 DAG and register →



Three proposed deliverables — protocol templates, a meeting worksheet, and reporting with a SET — and the reasoning each supports.

title: Proposal 1 · Update protocol templates
text:
Why update the templates?
The associations workflow produces a Summary of Evidence table (SET). The hypothesis-generating workflow already recommends a DAG and produces a Summary of Evidence on Mediators (SEM). The amendments connect the causal diagram, assumption register, and meeting record across both routes.
The retrospective TAAR1 example motivates the proposed changes:







Gap illustrated by the retrospective example
What the amendment addresses




Association and mechanism questions can occur in the same review.
Declare the review mode and the diagram’s purpose.


Pathways may be reconstructed after the findings.
Record the proposed structure and challenge conditions before synthesis.


The two template routes produce different evidence summaries.
Link both routes to the DAG and assumption register.


Meeting reasoning may remain implicit.
Preserve the assumptions, judgements, and revisions in a reusable record.

title: Proposal 1 · Update protocol templates
text:
What changes in each template?
The uploaded drafts frame all additions as recommendations. These practical prompts are a main methods contribution for review.








Template
Where the additions appear
Practical change proposed




Associations v3.2 draft
Research questions; reporting bias; evidence summary; triangulation meeting.
Declare the review mode, introduce a versioned DAG and register, record bias direction, and use the assumptions in meeting conclusions.


Hypothesis-generating v2.2 draft
DAG guidance; data extraction; SEM; bridge to triangulation; consensus meeting.
Version the existing DAG, extract assumption-relevant information, connect the SEM to the register, and prepare a SET-style input for triangulation.





Verbatim yellow-highlighted extracts — for template owners

The 25 highlighted paragraphs are reproduced without rewriting. The original Word drafts remain internal; a download of the proposed wording is provided below.

Associations v3.2 draftHypothesis-generating v2.2 draft



Research questions

Review mode and causal structure (recommended):
We recommend that you state the primary mode of the review: evaluating associations, hypothesis-generating, or a mixture of both. If any research question concerns mechanisms of action or hypothesised causal pathways, we recommend declaring this explicitly as a secondary (hypothesis-generating) mode.
We recommend that, in that case, you draw a scoping directed acyclic graph (DAG) at protocol stage: the variables of interest, the hypothesised directional links between them (including candidate mediators), and the outcome(s). The DAG is a working hypothesis, not a finding, and should be versioned (dated and archived).
We recommend that research questions about causal pathways are then answered edge by edge against the pre-specified DAG (i.e. “is the evidence consistent with this hypothesised link?”), rather than by reconstructing pathways after the findings.



Reporting bias

We recommend that, for each major bias, the likely direction of the resulting error is recorded relative to the relevant DAG edge (towards null, away from null, or unpredictable), in addition to the risk-of-bias judgement. Where quantitative bias adjustment is planned, the bias type can also be recorded: offset (additive) bias shifts every estimate by a roughly fixed amount and can create an effect where the true effect is zero, whereas scaling (proportional) bias inflates or shrinks estimates in proportion to their size and cannot.



Summary of the evidence

Making the Summary of Evidence (SET) table DAG-compatible (recommended):
We recommend adding the following fields to each row of the Summary of Evidence (SET) table: (i) which DAG edge(s) the evidence stream informs; (ii) up to three key assumptions on which the estimate depends, each typed as structural, identifying, indirectness or proxy, with status (agreed / contested / uncertain); (iii) the expected direction of each major bias relative to the relevant DAG edge (towards null / away from null / unpredictable); and (iv) a link to the versioned DAG and assumption register.
We recommend that the assumption register is seeded at protocol stage and versioned. Each entry records the assumption, its type, the evidence streams it concerns, its status, and what evidence would challenge it.



Triangulation meeting

Using the DAG and assumption register at the triangulation meeting (recommended):
We recommend that, before the meeting, each SET table row is mapped onto the DAG edge(s) it informs. Streams that inform different edges do not directly agree or disagree; any statement about agreement between them traverses an assumption (e.g. a proxy assumption) that should be named.
We recommend that conclusions are reported per DAG edge, with the traversed assumptions stated, rather than as a single global judgement.
We recommend that orthogonality is judged from the directions of the streams' major biases: streams whose biases favour findings in opposite directions (one towards null, one away from null) make agreement between them strongly informative. Representing each bias as a factor in the DAG makes this a checkable claim (the biases should share no common cause).
We recommend applying three revision triggers during the meeting: (a) evidence incompatible with a DAG edge; (b) an evidence stream that maps onto no edge; (c) an assumption challenged in discussion. Each trigger should lead to a versioned update of the DAG or assumption register.





DAG and assumption register

Versioning the DAG and attaching an assumption register (recommended):
We recommend that the DAG is treated as a versioned working model: it will be refined as evidence accumulates, and each version is dated and archived.
We recommend that, for each edge, you note which evidence streams (non-human, human observational, human interventional, mechanistic) can inform it.
We recommend attaching an assumption register to the DAG. For each assumption, record: its type (structural — an asserted causal link; identifying — what makes a stream's estimate causal; indirectness — how closely the stream's population, intervention and outcome match the target question, including animal-to-human relevance; proxy — a measured outcome standing in for the target outcome); its status (agreed / contested / uncertain); the streams it concerns; and what evidence would challenge it.



Data extraction

We recommend also extracting information relevant to the assumption register — for example the timing of mediator measurement, population characteristics, and intervention dose or exposure descriptors — so that indirectness and proxy assumptions can be re-evaluated as evidence accumulates, and not only effect estimates.



Summary of Evidence on Mediators (SEM)

Making the SEM DAG-compatible (recommended):
We recommend adding the following fields to the SEM for each candidate mediator: (i) which DAG edge(s) the evidence about it informs; (ii) up to three key assumptions (typed, and with status, as in the assumption register); and (iii) a link to the versioned DAG and assumption register.



Bridge to triangulation

Bridging to triangulation (recommended):
We recommend that, because this template produces a Summary of the Evidence on Mediators (SEM) rather than a Summary of Evidence (SET) table, teams preparing for triangulation derive a one-row-per-stream SET-style table from the DAG (using the fields described in the associations template) so that both template routes feed the triangulation meeting comparably.



Consensus meeting

Reviewing the assumption register at the consensus meeting (recommended):
We recommend that the assumption register is a standing agenda item: assumptions challenged by the accumulated evidence are re-statused (agreed / contested / uncertain), and the DAG is revised if a revision trigger fires (evidence incompatible with an edge; a stream that maps onto no edge; an assumption challenged in discussion).
We recommend that conclusions are reported per DAG edge, naming the assumptions they traverse. Note that a small mechanistic study that measures a node on a DAG edge can have probative value out of proportion to its precision, because it bears on whether an association is causal rather than confounded.

title: Proposal 1 · Update protocol templates
text:
Specifying the target quantity
The amendments above make the causal structure explicit; a companion step makes the quantity explicit. Companion guidance (Component A) helps a team specify what each question targets before eligibility and extraction are fixed. Questions are classed as descriptive, associational, causal or hypothesis-generating — a review can mix modes, and the mode does not determine the template route. The operational rule: a causal-mode question in the associations route triggers the DAG and register amendments, because that template contains no DAG by default; mechanistic or hypothesis-generating questions use the hypothesis route and link the SEM to the register. The specification extends PICO/PMICO rather than replacing it — each worksheet step maps to a familiar element, with the summary quantity, intercurrent events, effect type and evidence streams as explicit extensions.
The guidance also specifies a stream-level estimand for each evidence stream — the quantity that stream can estimate in its own terms — so that alignment at the evidence-summary stage relates two specified quantities rather than a study and an underspecified ambition. The TAAR1 page shows an illustrative completed target statement.


Specification worksheet, stream-level estimands, and governance


A3. Specification worksheet — review-team prompts
Copy this section into a review-specific note. Complete provisionally, discuss ambiguities, and revise after causal-structure discussion.








Step
Signalling question
Provisional answer / unresolved issue




1. Purpose
What decision or scientific explanation motivates the review?
To complete


2. Mode
Descriptive, association, causal, hypothesis-generating or mixed? Why?
To complete


3. Target population
Who or what should the answer apply to? Setting and eligibility?
To complete


4. Exposure/intervention
What are the relevant level(s), versions, duration and implementation?
To complete


5. Comparator
Compared with what observable or hypothetical alternative?
To complete


6. Outcome/construct
What is the target construct, and by what measure and direction?
To complete


7. Timing
When are exposure, mediator (if any) and outcome assessed?
To complete


8. Summary quantity
Risk difference/ratio, mean difference, prevalence, association slope, etc.?
To complete


9. Intercurrent events
Which events change interpretation/existence of outcome? Which strategy addresses them (if applicable)?
To complete


10. Effect type
Total effect? A specified direct or indirect effect? Conditional or marginal?
To complete


11. Evidence streams
Which streams might estimate the target? Which could inform related effects, pathways, context or assumptions?
To complete


12. Assumptions
What must be true to interpret or transport stream findings to this target?
To complete


13. Open questions
What still needs expert, stakeholder or methodological input?
To complete





Writing the target statement

Causal template: “In [target population], what is the [summary] of [outcome at time] under [intervention strategy] compared with [comparator strategy], treating [key intercurrent events] using [specified strategy]?”
Association template: “In [population and period], what is the [marginal/conditional association measure] between [defined exposure] and [outcome at time], with [conditioning variables/standardisation]?”
Descriptive template: “In [population/period], what proportion/mean [well-defined property] is observed, measured by [definition]?”
Hypothesis-generating template: “Which candidate variables or pathways might connect [exposure] and [outcome], and what forms of evidence could support or challenge the proposed relationships?”

These are templates for clarification, not guarantees of identification.


Specifying stream-level estimands (A3a)
For each evidence stream nominated in worksheet step 11, specify the quantity that stream can estimate in its own terms. Illustrative TAAR1 application (placeholders to be confirmed against the included studies; not a completed assessment):








Field
Human stream (TAAR1, illustrative)
Animal stream (TAAR1, illustrative)




Population
Adults with schizophrenia spectrum disorders in the included trials
The strains, sexes and challenge paradigms used in the included experiments


Intervention/exposure
Add-on TAAR1 agonist at trial doses
Compound at preclinical doses in a challenge-induced state


Comparator
Placebo add-on (or as reported)
Vehicle under challenge


Outcome/construct
PANSS total (a measure of the symptom construct)
Reversal of challenge-induced hyperlocomotion (a behavioural outcome)


Timing
4–6 weeks
As reported per paradigm


Summary quantity
As reported (e.g. mean difference, SMD)
As reported (e.g. SMD)


Effect type
Assignment effect under the trials’ strategies (to confirm)
Experimental contrast under each study’s design



The proxy assumption A1 is then a bridge between two specified estimands — a claim that the animal stream’s quantity is informative about the human stream’s construct — rather than a vague link between “animal studies” and “the human question”.


Governance of the target statement (proposal)

Drafting: the review team drafts the target statement and stream-level estimands at protocol stage, using the worksheet.
Sign-off: agreed with clinical, preclinical and methodological input before eligibility screening begins; experiential and stakeholder input informs outcomes and contrasts.
Amendment: any change after sign-off requires a version increment, a dated justification, and a note of the evidence known at the time.
Disagreement: record disagreement and the positions held in the register rather than forcing consensus; unresolved disagreement is carried into triangulation as an explicit condition on interpretation.

These arrangements are proposals for discussion; GALENOS governance groups should confirm ownership and process.

Proposed template

Review / evidence stream.
Outcome, contrast, estimate and uncertainty, or qualitative summary.
Within-study risk of bias and expected direction.
Reporting-bias assessment and expected direction.
Relevance to the target population, species, model, exposure, or outcome.
Relevant issues not covered elsewhere.
Relationship informed; up to three typed assumptions and status; links to the versioned DAG and register.




Below the table: state the meeting conclusion, the assumptions it depends on, and unresolved questions. The existing bias and indirectness columns retain their roles; the added column connects those judgements to the causal model.
Alignment is recorded below the table, not in it. The Key Assumptions column holds only the relationship informed, typed assumption IDs with status, and links. Below the table, one short narrative record per stream row asks whether the stream estimated the review’s target quantity at all — a different judgement from indirectness, which asks whether the estimate applies to the target population, exposure or outcome. A stream can be low in indirectness for its own estimand yet misaligned with the review target (the TAAR1 animal behavioural outcome), or closely aligned in quantity yet indirect for the target population.


Worked alignment narrative — TAAR1 animal stream

Illustrative narrative record — TAAR1 animal stream (retrospective reconstruction, for calibration only; not a completed assessment):

SET row and target reference: TAAR1 animal experimental evidence; target version [draft specification, Component A §A5].
Stream-level estimand: Effect of [compound] versus vehicle on reversal of challenge-induced hyperlocomotion in [strains/paradigms as included], reported as [SMD].
What is being summarised? Experimental contrasts across animal studies; the synthesis summarises a distribution of animal-specific effects, not the human clinical quantity.
Main points of alignment or difference: Different population (species, challenge state), different intervention (preclinical dosing), different outcome (locomotor behaviour versus PANSS-assessed symptoms), different effect definition (experimental contrast, not a treatment-policy effect).
Why this evidence contributes: Related-effect and mechanistic contribution; informs the proposed pathway and the behavioural-proxy assumption rather than the clinical target directly.
What must be assumed to connect it to the target? A1 (behavioural proxy validity, contested) and A2 (dose/compound applicability, contested).
Unresolved questions for triangulation: Whether proxy validity can be evaluated empirically; whether shared biases (for example, publication practices or selective outcome reporting operating across species) could produce concordant directions.

title: Proposal 3 · Reporting and the Summary of Evidence table
text:
Reporting the meeting outcome
The proposed wording makes the conditional interpretation explicit. For TAAR1, the key point is that a judgement about human symptoms cannot treat the animal proxy as the same measured outcome.







Situation
Suggested sentence structure




Contributions support the same interpretation
“Evidence from [streams] is consistent with [interpretation], conditional on [assumptions].”


Agreement may reflect shared bias
“The findings agree, but shared bias through [mechanism] remains a possible explanation.”


Related but non-identical effects (integration level B)
“The [animal] and [human] streams address related but non-identical outcomes; their estimates are compared but not pooled, and their consistency is conditional on [assumption].”


Complementary contributions (integration level C)
“The streams inform different links in the causal pathway and are interpreted as complementary; together they [support / leave uncertain] the proposed explanation, conditional on [assumptions].”


Contributions diverge
“The findings diverge for [relationship]; differences in [estimands, applicability, or bias] remain unresolved.”



Preserving magnitude and uncertainty. Conclusions about agreement or divergence must preserve or point to effect magnitude and uncertainty (for example, the estimate with its confidence interval), not direction alone; a summary estimate should not be reduced to a qualitative claim such as “supports efficacy”.


Detailed questions for follow-up


Does Key Assumptions provide enough information without crowding the existing table?
Which wording examples need design-specific guidance?


The four questions on the Briefing page guide the meeting discussion.

title: LSR8 · Heat & Mental Health
text:
Priority adjudications



Issue
Why the decision matters




Medication use and social support
Their proposed roles may differ with temporal ordering; treating them as confounders, or shared causes of exposure and outcome, by default could change the quantity estimated.


Cooling-to-heat applicability (A7)
Determines the contribution cooling RCTs can make to the target heat question. Deciding what the target quantity is — an observed association or a defined intervention effect — is the kind of question the estimand specification guidance is designed to settle before synthesis.


Ambient temperature versus extreme heat (A3)
Determines whether the two exposure constructs require distinct comparisons and interpretation.


Animal proxy and duration eligibility (A1–A2)
Determines what animal evidence is eligible and how it could inform human outcomes.


Depression and suicidality (A9)
Requires clarity on whether a line represents a causal hypothesis or a descriptive association. A correlation annotation is not a causal DAG edge.

title: LSR8 · Heat & Mental Health
text:
Applying the three proposals
As the Summary of Evidence tables (SETs) become available, use them to examine what each stream informs and which assumptions require revision.

Establish the baseline: record when the framework entered use, the available evidence, and which choices restate or extend the protocol.
Use the worksheet: record the interpretation, disputed assumptions, revisions, and actions through the four steps.
Carry the judgement forward: link the reported conclusion to the diagram, register, and evidence-summary versions used.

Detailed questions for follow-up — evaluation

These are candidate observations for a pilot, not additional questions for the initial meeting.

Which assumptions or disagreements become more explicit, and do participants find that useful?
Does the contribution map change how a stream is interpreted or which conclusion is considered warranted?
How much preparation and meeting time is needed, and where is information duplicated?
Can the record be maintained at the next update, with clear ownership and traceable revisions?
What feedback do methodological, statistical, clinical, and lived-experience contributors give on its clarity?




Project materials and implementation details

The project materials include the completed protocol, draft DAG package v1.1, an assumption register, a provisional covariate-adjudication table, and a prefilled worksheet. The protocol records registration on 30 March 2026 (PROSPERO 1325620).
Evidence availability in those records is a dated snapshot. Current SET availability, the adoption date, meeting plans, and register ownership need confirmation with the review team. No effect estimates or meeting judgements are entered here.
The protocol makes convening a triangulation meeting conditional on sufficient evidence from at least two sources for an outcome. The register and evidence-gap record can be prepared before that condition is met.


The figures and working assumptions follow the draft LSR8 DAG package v1.1. Application status and provenance. The Briefing page holds the meeting questions.
